source.title: Rotational Equilibrium: How Weight Decay Balances Learning Across Neural Networks
source.authors: Atli Kosson; Bettina Messmer; Martin Jaggi

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper and appendices; no material truncation is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports held-out performance comparisons that qualify optimizer and batch-size claims, but it does not measure the train–test gap or test memorization of random labels.
record.gate_note: The paper studies optimizer dynamics and weight decay, not generalization as a train–test gap. Its optimizer and batch-size results report held-out metrics and bear on V4 and V5. Its discussion of other studies is not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study explicitly reproduces the AdamW-versus-Adam+ℓ2 hyperparameter sweep with a different ResNet and training duration, testing V4's decoupled-weight-decay clause. Its baseline results also bear on V4's optimizer comparison and V5's fixed-epoch batch-size effect.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that weight decay regulates neuronal update dynamics across components and time, and that balanced rotation helps explain benefits of AdamW and normalization. Explicit rotational control can reproduce weight-decay benefits and reduce warmup dependence. They present balanced rotation as an empirically useful heuristic, not a proven generalization mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and experimentally changes weight-decay and rotational-update dynamics; it does not reproduce the original generalization experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Held-out performance differs with optimizer variant and batch size; the paper also reports effects of learning-rate and weight-decay choices, but those are not direct tests of the listed gap claims.

fits_no_version.finding: Disabling weight decay degrades several baselines, while rotational optimizer variants often recover their performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Controlling average neuronal angular updates can reproduce benefits of weight decay in the tested training recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 18 reports lower validation accuracy when ResNet-18 width is reduced, but does not establish a zero-training-error threshold or convergence without explicit regularization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider ResNet-18 variants perform better within the tested regularized rotational-optimizer setup.

fits_no_version.finding: Warmup substantially improves large-batch SGDM training, while rotational variants depend much less on warmup; no matched small-batch comparison establishes closure of a batch-size penalty.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Directly controlling rotation reduces warmup dependence in the tested image-classification and language-model recipes.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 235, 2024
record.problems: The paper measures held-out performance, not training error or the train–test gap. Batch-size comparisons use different learning-rate settings, so batch size is not isolated. The AdamW versus Adam+ℓ2 evidence is one image-classification task and compares two adaptive methods.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows from the appendix optimizer sweeps or figure-only results were extracted: their detailed per-condition values are not recoverable as exact results from the supplied text, and the table comparisons above cover the tested V4 and V5 claims.

untested.parts: Fitting fixed random labels and comparing natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Widening beyond a demonstrated zero-training-error threshold under convergence training without explicit regularization.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.

The ResNet-20 baseline comparisons do not document matched tuning budgets restricted to learning rates and decay schedules. Equal or better adaptive-method training performance, recovery to SGD performance through decoupled weight decay, broader-tuning reversals, Adam-to-SGD switching, and adaptive-versus-SGD language-model comparisons are untested.

Language-model batch-size sweeps, identification of a workload-dependent batch threshold, and controlled demonstrations that longer training or recipe adaptations close the small-versus-large-batch penalty.
Controlled dropout additions or removals, training-set-size dependence, excessive dropout, and joint dropout/weight-decay removal with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, its correlation with train–test gaps, and comparison with norm- or margin-based rankings.
Influence-based identification and removal of memorized training examples followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. Held-out performance suffices to test V4 and V5; a measured train–test gap is not required. Batch-size comparisons use different learning rates, so verdicts apply to the reported recipes rather than an isolated batch-size intervention. Appendix J reports a slightly different AdamW baseline, 94.71±0.16%, from Appendix K's 94.74±0.14%; R2 correctly follows its cited Appendix K result.

versions.untested_parts: Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Comparisons with SGD or momentum SGD under limited tuning; language benchmarks where Adam does better; broader tuning and optimizer-switching results.
Large-batch effects for language models; longer training, warmup, normalization, or regularization adaptations as controlled comparisons to the same recipe.
Dropout interventions and their effects across training-set sizes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the train–test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

relation.reason: The study reports its own AdamW-versus-Adam+L2 results and optimizer/batch-size baseline accuracies bearing directly on V4 and V5.

tranche.reason: Section 5.3 and Appendix K explicitly reproduce the original AdamW-versus-Adam+L2 learning-rate/regularization sweep and held-out accuracy comparison, changing the network and training duration.
